bull_bear.body:
- integration: single contractor from the seam to the rake — mining, overburden removal, loading, road transport and rail rake loading on one owned fleet and workforce, which the AR says lets it optimise plant and machinery utilisation and bid at more competitive rates — evidence: provides coal extraction, overburden removal, coal loading/unloading, road transportation, rake loading and rail coordination; iron ore logistics uses the same tippers, drivers, diesel contracts and workshops as coal — against it: the logistics business is 'well under one per cent of the mineral logistics market', and coal transported by road fell from 12.47 MT to 8.50 MT and coal loaded on rakes from 22.51 MT to 11.37 MT between Fiscal 2025 and Fiscal 2026
- scale: an owned, pre-funded fleet, which the AR names as the practical entry barrier (a bidder must own a fleet and fund it before the first contract is awarded) — evidence: owned 1,781 and leased 100 vehicles, plant and machinery at 31 March 2026, including 863 mining tippers, 362 tip trailers, 159 excavators, 64 loaders, 62 bulldozers and 32 graders; contract mining market share rose from under 1% in Fiscal 2020 to about 5.1% in Fiscal 2026 and share of Coal India contractual overburden removal from 1.9% in Fiscal 2022 to 6.6% — against it: 'Some competitors may have greater financial and technological resources', and the fleet is funded primarily through bank term loans
- cost position: in-house fleet maintenance — evidence: maintenance and preventive maintenance is carried out in house at its own workshops at the Chandrapur headquarters and at seven mining sites
- cost position: diesel bought in advance directly from refineries, with price variation clauses in mining and logistics work orders — evidence: 'the Company typically purchases its diesel requirements in advance directly from refineries'; 'Mining and logistics work orders carry price variation clauses' — against it: the Company 'has not historically hedged, and does not currently hedge, its diesel price risk', and diesel is its single largest expense category
bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Customer concentration in two Coal India subsidiaries — WCL and NCL are the largest mining customers; the top 10 customers gave 98.40% of Fiscal 2026 revenue and the top 20 gave 99.69%. The Board lists dependence on a limited number of large customers among its key monitored risks.
- Diesel price volatility, unhedged — Power and fuel, mostly diesel, is the single largest expense. Work orders carry price variation clauses, but the Company does not hedge; if it cannot absorb or pass on higher costs, results, cash flows and borrowing needs are hit.
- Capital intensity and cost of funding — Growth needs substantial, continuing spend on trucks, equipment and machinery, funded mainly by bank term loans. Failing to raise funds on time could stop it servicing new projects, and more debt brings higher interest and restrictive covenants.
- Competitive, uncertain tendering and contract renewal — Mining contracts, mainly from Coal India and its subsidiaries, are won through competitive bidding, and the Board lists contract-renewal and tendering risk among its key risks. Some competitors have greater financial and technological resources, and more competition may reduce revenue, margins or market share.
- Dependence on coal demand and the macro cycle — Growth is tied to end-customer demand for contract mining and logistics, which depends on the macroeconomic factors behind coal consumption. Performance may soften in recessions.
- Seasonality and monsoon disruption — An abnormal monsoon materially affects operations. Activity is lower in the monsoon-affected first and second quarters, partly offset in the third and fourth.
- Semi-fixed employee cost base — Employee costs are semi-fixed. If revenue grows more slowly than the headcount hired for new projects, margins could come under pressure.
- Regulatory, fleet-breakdown and financial risks — The Board monitors regulatory risk from coal mining and environmental laws, fleet and equipment breakdown, IT and cyber-security risk, and interest-rate, credit and liquidity risk.

business.body: Caliber Mining and Logistics is an integrated mining services operator that manages overburden removal, coal extraction and coal logistics as a single, end-to-end offering, executed on contract at customer-owned open-cast coal mines in Maharashtra and Madhya Pradesh. Its largest mining customers are Western Coalfields Limited and Northern Coalfields Limited, both Coal India subsidiaries, and it also provides coal and iron ore loading, unloading, road transportation, rail rake loading and rail coordination to power and industrial customers, plus a small coal trading line. It runs an owned fleet of tippers, excavators, loaders, bulldozers and graders maintained in its own workshops.

outlook.body:
- Keep expanding the mining business with Coal India, bidding for new contracts with WCL, NCL and other Coal India subsidiaries on the strength of its coal-region footprint, logistics experience and the plant and machinery already in place.
- Move into the coal regions where incremental production is concentrated: tendering in Odisha and Jharkhand, and a joint venture that takes the Company to Central Coalfields for the first time.
- Build early, explicitly small positions outside coal: two wholly owned subsidiaries whose objects extend to iron ore, coking coal, manganese and limestone, and a 40% stake in an SPV for a critical mineral mining project; management states 'The core will remain coal for a long time.'
- Serve the whole value chain as an integrated contract-mining and logistics provider, using combined fleet and manpower to improve utilisation and bid more competitively.
- Add fleet (trucks, equipment and machinery) contract by contract as new mining awards come in, funded by operating cash flow, bank borrowings and overdraft facilities.
- Deleverage using IPO proceeds: prepay fleet loans and retire higher-cost debt across fifteen lenders.

outlook.body: Fiscal 2026 was a fleet-building year: the Company added vehicles, tippers, excavators and other machinery to service newly awarded mining and logistics contracts, funded by operating cash flow and bank term loans, and management says it is adding more fleet capacity in Fiscal 2027. Two new sites, Dudhichua and Gouri Pouni New, started during the year and are still below the run rate their contracts imply; Gouri Pouni New runs to 2031, and Sasti and Dudhichua to 2029. Headcount rose to support three new mining contracts, with maintenance staff growing alongside the fleet, and the ERP system was extended to track stores and spares. Further fleet will be bought contract by contract as new mining awards come in, and part of the IPO fresh-issue proceeds is earmarked for buying commercial vehicles and plant and machinery. The Company is also bidding in Odisha and Jharkhand.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- India's raw coal production is expected to rise from 1,048 million tonnes in Fiscal 2025 to 1,484 million tonnes by Fiscal 2030; coal's share of electricity falls but coal-based generation still rises in absolute terms.
- Contract mining awards depend on contractors being able to show that machines and crews already exist; the Company says the capital deployed in Fiscal 2026 is what allowed it to bid.
- Returns on capital and equity are expected to strengthen as the assets commissioned in Fiscal 2026 (many late in the year) reach full contribution from Fiscal 2027.
- Employee costs are semi-fixed; management expects employee and other operating costs as a share of revenue to stabilise as revenue expands.
- Offer proceeds used to prepay fleet loans are expected to cut finance costs.
- Diesel procurement discipline and in-house workshops are cited as the operating levers behind cost efficiency across a larger fleet.
- Order book (including advance work orders) of ₹5,66,829.69 lakhs at 31 March 2026, up 33.61% over the year; 93.27% contract coal mining and overburden removal, 6.73% logistics.
- Order book reached ₹9,55,089.08 lakhs by 15 May 2026 after further awards at Dhoptala, Dudhichua and Jayant; 95.90% coal mining and overburden removal.
- Anticipated execution periods of 32 to 68 months for mining and overburden removal contracts and 12 to 60 months for logistics contracts, which management says gives revenue visibility over the medium term.
- Chairman describes the May 2026 order book as close to six times Fiscal 2026 revenue.

concerns_observed: Extreme customer concentration: top 3 customers = 90.11% of FY26 revenue, single largest (NCL) 44.16%; top 10 = 98.40%. Standard-form WCL/NCL contracts favour the counterparty (no liability cap in some, customer termination and tender-barring rights, latent site-defect risk with no recourse).

Asset-light on the underlying resource: the Company owns no mines or coal reserves and depends on winning/renewing 2-3 year contracts; contracts over Rs 1,000 cr each contributed 76.12% of FY26 revenue.

High leverage: aggregate borrowings Rs 1,057.61 cr at March 31, 2026 (D/E 1.63x; 1.33x FY25, 2.45x FY24), DSCR a thin 1.12x, finance cost Rs 81.25 cr; Rs 208 cr of Net Proceeds is earmarked to repay borrowings.

Diesel-dependent, fixed-rate margin exposure: power and fuel was 53.51% of total expenses (Rs 783.91 cr) in FY26; mining is mostly on fixed rates with only partial escalation cover, and diesel is exposed to global energy prices.
Contingent liabilities of Rs 458.53 cr = 70.81% of net worth at FY26 (up from 28.51% FY25), predominantly bank guarantees of Rs 440.14 cr.

Heavy related-party dependence: sale of services to related parties was Rs 271.84 cr (16.35% of FY26 revenue), including KSR Freight Carriers - a partnership of all Promoters that is simultaneously a top-3 customer (5.00% of revenue); logistics services are taken from Shree Chadda Roadlines, for which the Company also gave a corporate guarantee.

Execution risk on capex object: Rs 167 cr of the fresh issue is for commercial vehicles/plant & machinery for which 100% of orders are not yet placed, and deployment has not been appraised by any bank or financial institution.
Structural end-market risk: thermal (non-coking) coal for power generation is the end-use for most output, exposing volumes to the renewable-energy transition.
Family-controlled: Promoters hold 88.75% pre-Offer and all four executive directors are from the Chadda family.

Owned, integrated fleet of 1,911 vehicles/plant & machinery (100 leased) with in-house maintenance at seven mining-site workshops, direct month-ahead diesel procurement, and ERP across operations - supporting cost and scheduling control.

Independent directors with direct sector pedigree: ex-Chairman of Coal India (Anil Kumar Jha) and ex-Director (Finance) of Western Coalfields (Rajendra Prasad Shukla), on an 8-member board with 4 independents.

cost_leadership.title: Supply chain integration (RHP report)
cost_leadership.body: Integrated end-to-end coal mining and logistics services provider offering coal extraction, overburden removal, coal loading and unloading, road transportation and coordination of rail transportation as a one-stop provider. Owns its fleet (1,811 owned and 100 leased vehicles, plant and machinery as of April 30, 2026), enabling cost, scheduling and customer-service advantages over leased fleets. Conducts in-house and preventive maintenance at its own workshops (headquarters at Chandrapur plus seven mining sites), providing cost savings. demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- India's raw coal production is expected to rise from 1,048 million tonnes in Fiscal 2025 to 1,484 million tonnes by Fiscal 2030; coal's share of electricity falls but coal-based generation still rises in absolute terms.
- Contract mining awards depend on contractors being able to show that machines and crews already exist; the Company says the capital deployed in Fiscal 2026 is what allowed it to bid.
- Returns on capital and equity are expected to strengthen as the assets commissioned in Fiscal 2026 (many late in the year) reach full contribution from Fiscal 2027.
- Employee costs are semi-fixed; management expects employee and other operating costs as a share of revenue to stabilise as revenue expands.
- Offer proceeds used to prepay fleet loans are expected to cut finance costs.
- Diesel procurement discipline and in-house workshops are cited as the operating levers behind cost efficiency across a larger fleet.
- Order book (including advance work orders) of ₹5,66,829.69 lakhs at 31 March 2026, up 33.61% over the year; 93.27% contract coal mining and overburden removal, 6.73% logistics.
- Order book reached ₹9,55,089.08 lakhs by 15 May 2026 after further awards at Dhoptala, Dudhichua and Jayant; 95.90% coal mining and overburden removal.
- Anticipated execution periods of 32 to 68 months for mining and overburden removal contracts and 12 to 60 months for logistics contracts, which management says gives revenue visibility over the medium term.
- Chairman describes the May 2026 order book as close to six times Fiscal 2026 revenue.

capital_allocation.title: Strategy & capital allocation
capital_allocation.body:
- Keep expanding the mining business with Coal India, bidding for new contracts with WCL, NCL and other Coal India subsidiaries on the strength of its coal-region footprint, logistics experience and the plant and machinery already in place.
- Move into the coal regions where incremental production is concentrated: tendering in Odisha and Jharkhand, and a joint venture that takes the Company to Central Coalfields for the first time.
- Build early, explicitly small positions outside coal: two wholly owned subsidiaries whose objects extend to iron ore, coking coal, manganese and limestone, and a 40% stake in an SPV for a critical mineral mining project; management states 'The core will remain coal for a long time.'
- Serve the whole value chain as an integrated contract-mining and logistics provider, using combined fleet and manpower to improve utilisation and bid more competitively.
- Add fleet (trucks, equipment and machinery) contract by contract as new mining awards come in, funded by operating cash flow, bank borrowings and overdraft facilities.
- Deleverage using IPO proceeds: prepay fleet loans and retire higher-cost debt across fifteen lenders.

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: Fiscal 2026 was a fleet-building year: the Company added vehicles, tippers, excavators and other machinery to service newly awarded mining and logistics contracts, funded by operating cash flow and bank term loans, and management says it is adding more fleet capacity in Fiscal 2027. Two new sites, Dudhichua and Gouri Pouni New, started during the year and are still below the run rate their contracts imply; Gouri Pouni New runs to 2031, and Sasti and Dudhichua to 2029. Headcount rose to support three new mining contracts, with maintenance staff growing alongside the fleet, and the ERP system was extended to track stores and spares. Further fleet will be bought contract by contract as new mining awards come in, and part of the IPO fresh-issue proceeds is earmarked for buying commercial vehicles and plant and machinery. The Company is also bidding in Odisha and Jharkhand.

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- integration: single contractor from the seam to the rake — mining, overburden removal, loading, road transport and rail rake loading on one owned fleet and workforce, which the AR says lets it optimise plant and machinery utilisation and bid at more competitive rates — evidence: provides coal extraction, overburden removal, coal loading/unloading, road transportation, rake loading and rail coordination; iron ore logistics uses the same tippers, drivers, diesel contracts and workshops as coal — against it: the logistics business is 'well under one per cent of the mineral logistics market', and coal transported by road fell from 12.47 MT to 8.50 MT and coal loaded on rakes from 22.51 MT to 11.37 MT between Fiscal 2025 and Fiscal 2026
- scale: an owned, pre-funded fleet, which the AR names as the practical entry barrier (a bidder must own a fleet and fund it before the first contract is awarded) — evidence: owned 1,781 and leased 100 vehicles, plant and machinery at 31 March 2026, including 863 mining tippers, 362 tip trailers, 159 excavators, 64 loaders, 62 bulldozers and 32 graders; contract mining market share rose from under 1% in Fiscal 2020 to about 5.1% in Fiscal 2026 and share of Coal India contractual overburden removal from 1.9% in Fiscal 2022 to 6.6% — against it: 'Some competitors may have greater financial and technological resources', and the fleet is funded primarily through bank term loans
- cost position: in-house fleet maintenance — evidence: maintenance and preventive maintenance is carried out in house at its own workshops at the Chandrapur headquarters and at seven mining sites
- cost position: diesel bought in advance directly from refineries, with price variation clauses in mining and logistics work orders — evidence: 'the Company typically purchases its diesel requirements in advance directly from refineries'; 'Mining and logistics work orders carry price variation clauses' — against it: the Company 'has not historically hedged, and does not currently hedge, its diesel price risk', and diesel is its single largest expense category

risks.title: Bear — key risks
risks.body:
- Customer concentration in two Coal India subsidiaries — WCL and NCL are the largest mining customers; the top 10 customers gave 98.40% of Fiscal 2026 revenue and the top 20 gave 99.69%. The Board lists dependence on a limited number of large customers among its key monitored risks.
- Diesel price volatility, unhedged — Power and fuel, mostly diesel, is the single largest expense. Work orders carry price variation clauses, but the Company does not hedge; if it cannot absorb or pass on higher costs, results, cash flows and borrowing needs are hit.
- Capital intensity and cost of funding — Growth needs substantial, continuing spend on trucks, equipment and machinery, funded mainly by bank term loans. Failing to raise funds on time could stop it servicing new projects, and more debt brings higher interest and restrictive covenants.
- Competitive, uncertain tendering and contract renewal — Mining contracts, mainly from Coal India and its subsidiaries, are won through competitive bidding, and the Board lists contract-renewal and tendering risk among its key risks. Some competitors have greater financial and technological resources, and more competition may reduce revenue, margins or market share.
- Dependence on coal demand and the macro cycle — Growth is tied to end-customer demand for contract mining and logistics, which depends on the macroeconomic factors behind coal consumption. Performance may soften in recessions.
- Seasonality and monsoon disruption — An abnormal monsoon materially affects operations. Activity is lower in the monsoon-affected first and second quarters, partly offset in the third and fourth.
- Semi-fixed employee cost base — Employee costs are semi-fixed. If revenue grows more slowly than the headcount hired for new projects, margins could come under pressure.
- Regulatory, fleet-breakdown and financial risks — The Board monitors regulatory risk from coal mining and environmental laws, fleet and equipment breakdown, IT and cyber-security risk, and interest-rate, credit and liquidity risk.
